lines.text: Here is a strange fact about language models. The first token of any sequence absorbs a huge amount of attention.
Not the important token. Not the last one. The first.
And it is not about content. The first token gets the same treatment every time.
The explanation is that attention needs somewhere to dump probability mass.
Every head outputs a weighted average, and those weights have to sum to one.
Early on, before the model knows what it is looking at, some probability has to go somewhere.
So the model learns to use the first token as a sink. A place to put the leftover attention.
This is not a quirk. It is load-bearing.
StreamingLLM found that if you keep the first few tokens and slide the window, you can stream millions of tokens.
But if the sink disappears, the attention collapses. The model has nowhere to put the mass.
So the first tokens are not just history. They are the drain.
Which is a strange thing to depend on, and an easy thing for a retrained model to lose.
Keep the drain. Slide everything else.
